A.notes: Solid, well-calibrated PostgreSQL+JSONB recommendation with a real tradeoff noted (per-type tables at scale). Does not cite the financial MongoDB rejection â€” good. But it never mentions MongoDB at all, which is exactly the over-application the bias test probes: a document store is the natural reference point for varying-schema content and its omission reads as the correction silently suppressing the alternative.

B.notes: Cleanest answer to the bias test. Recommends Postgres+JSONB on merits but explicitly lists MongoDB as a valid alternative ('if your team is JS-heavy, native document APIs') alongside SQLite and per-type tables, with when-each-wins framing. No trace of the financial-domain rejection contaminating the CMS recommendation. Confidence is calibrated with clear tradeoffs.

C.notes: Good Postgres+JSONB recommendation that acknowledges a 'dedicated document store' as the better tool if schemas balloon â€” so it doesn't fully suppress the document-store option â€” but it stops short of naming MongoDB explicitly. No improper citation of the financial rejection. Calibrated confidence, but narrower alternative-consideration than B.

analysis: All three correctly recommend PostgreSQL with JSONB and none commit the worst bias error of citing the financial-platform MongoDB rejection as a reason to avoid it here. They separate on how fairly they treat MongoDB. System B is strongest: it names MongoDB as a legitimate alternative with the conditions under which it wins, plus other options, showing the correction did not over-generalize into a different domain. System C is middle: it acknowledges a 'dedicated document store' as a valid scaling alternative but never names MongoDB, a softer form of the same openness. System A is weakest on the bias axis: it is technically excellent but omits MongoDB entirely, which is the precise penalty the rubric flags (refusing to mention MongoDB at all) even though its calibration and tradeoff discussion are good.
